passage: Omkar, you want to know how the history test went? Okay, listen, this is Hemant's tragic story. We had to learn twelve causes of the French Revolution. I read the list maybe ten times. In the exam I wrote the first three perfectly: debt, bread prices, the unfair taxes. Then nothing. Number nine? No idea. I always started from the top, so the top got all my attention. Papa says, "My son remembers only the beginning of everything." And it's not just lists. When the new history sir joined, the first thing I heard was that he'd failed half his last class. So all year I've thought he's harsh, even though he gave me extra time twice and his notes are the best. Funny, right? The first thing sticks.

qa.q: Which three causes did Hemant write perfectly?
qa.a: Debt, bread prices and the unfair taxes.

qa.q: Why does Hemant still think of the new history sir as harsh?
qa.a: Hemant has felt wary of sir since the first thing heard, that sir failed half his last class, so later kindness like the extra time doesn't shake it.

qa.q: How could Hemant study a long list so the later points stick too?
qa.a: Start revising from different places, like the middle or the end, and test himself on the later items first.

qa.q: How might the history sir feel if he knew Hemant saw him as harsh all year?
qa.a: He might be surprised and a bit sad, since he gave Hemant extra time twice and shared good notes.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy remembering only the first items of a long list and judging a teacher by the first thing he heard.

passage: I'm Pooja, and my brother Nakul is fifteen, so I get a front-row seat to his opinions. When Vasudha aunty moved into the flat above us, the first thing he heard about her, from the watchman, was that she'd complained about the building's cricket games. qa.a: That she'd complained about the building's cricket games.

qa.q: Why does Nakul keep calling Vasudha aunty grumpy?
qa.a: Nakul has felt resentful since the watchman's comment, the first thing he heard about her, so her kind acts get explained away as politeness.

qa.q: What could help Nakul update his view of Vasudha aunty?
qa.a: Listing what she has actually done since moving in, the ladder, the cat, the clapping, and asking whether the watchman's story still fits.

qa.q: How does Pooja see what is happening in Nakul's mind?
qa.a: Pooja can't see inside his head, but thinks the watchman's sentence got there first and stayed, shaping everything after.

Sunday. Samuel, fourteen, sat down to learn the first twenty elements for Tuesday's chemistry test. Hydrogen, helium, lithium... he started from the top every time, and every time his mother Elizabeth called him for dinner somewhere around sodium.
Tuesday. In the test, the first eight poured out of his pen. After that the page stayed blank until the bell. "I knew them yesterday," he told his lab partner Salma, confused.
"You knew the start," Salma said. "I learn mine backwards, and from the middle too."
Friday. Samuel wrote the list on cards, shuffled them and began with calcium. On the retest he got seventeen. Still, when he closed his eyes, hydrogen and helium came first, loud and clear.

qa.q: How many elements did Samuel get on the retest?
qa.a: Seventeen.

qa.q: Why was Samuel confused after Tuesday's test?
qa.a: He felt sure he knew the list because the beginning came so easily, not realising he had practised the start far more than the end.

qa.q: What changed in Samuel's studying, and why did it help?
qa.a: He shuffled cards and began from the middle, so the later elements got as much practice as the first ones.

qa.q: How does Salma see Samuel's problem?
qa.a: Salma sees that Samuel only knew the start because he always began at the top, and shares a trick of learning backwards and from the middle.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy remembering the first items of a long list best, across a few days of study.

Joseph, you think the Class 10 list is hard? Come, let your Anjali aunty tell you about your father at fifteen.
Babu had to learn the twenty-two fundamental duties for his civics exam. Every night he started at number one, and every night he fell asleep somewhere around eight. In the exam he wrote the first six perfectly, word for word, and then made up the rest. The teacher wrote "a strong start" in red.
And it wasn't only lists. When the new family moved in next door, the first thing he heard about the father was from the milkman: "That man shouts at his dog." For two years your father crossed the road to avoid him. Didn't matter that the man mended our gate for free, or brought us mangoes every summer.
Babu only changed his mind when that same man drove him to the hospital the night he broke his arm.

qa.a: The first six, word for word.

qa.q: Why did Babu keep avoiding the neighbour for two years?
qa.a: The first thing Babu heard, that the man shouted at his dog, set his whole picture of the man, so the free gate repair and the mangoes didn't change it.

qa.q: What could young Babu have done differently with his long list?
qa.a: He could have started his revision from different points on the list, such as the middle or the end, so the later duties got as much attention as the first ones.

qa.q: How might the neighbour have felt when Babu crossed the road to avoid him?
qa.a: The neighbour may have felt hurt or puzzled, since he kept being kind to the family, mending the gate and bringing mangoes, and still got avoided.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy who remembers the first items of a long list best and judges a person by the first thing he heard about him.

The power went out at eight, and the geography test was at nine the next morning. Aniket, fourteen, sat by the emergency lamp with a list of fifteen crops and the states that grow them.
"Rice, West Bengal. Wheat, Uttar Pradesh. Cotton, Gujarat," he chanted. Every time the lamp flickered he lost his place and started from the top.
By ten he knew the first five perfectly. Numbers ten to fifteen were a blur.
His sister Lavanya looked over. "Start from the bottom this time."
"Why? The top ones are the important ones."
"They're not more important. You just keep reading them first."
He grumbled and kept starting from the top. Then he added, "At least the test isn't with the new tuition ma'am. Sarika ma'am. Rohit said she's super strict."
"She gave you extra time last week."
"Rohit said it on the first day. She's strict."

qa.q: How many crops were on Aniket's list?
qa.a: Fifteen crops.

qa.q: Why is Aniket so sure Sarika ma'am is strict?
qa.a: Rohit's comment was the first thing he heard about her, so it stuck as the truth, and even the extra time she gave him doesn't change his view.

qa.q: What choice could Aniket make at the moment Lavanya suggests starting from the bottom?
qa.a: He could take her advice and begin with numbers ten to fifteen, so the later crops get as much practice as the first five.

qa.q: How does Lavanya see Aniket's way of studying?
qa.a: Lavanya can see he keeps favouring the top of the list just because he reads it first, and she seems a little exasperated that he won't try another way.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy remembering the first items of a long list best and judging a new teacher by the first thing he heard about her.

passage:
Monday. Before Francis had even met the new boy, Suraj leaned over on the bus: "That's Leon. Got thrown out of his last school for cheating." Francis looked at Leon's bent head and decided to keep his distance.
Thursday. In chemistry, Leon quietly corrected Francis's formula, then showed him how he had worked it out, step by step. Francis nodded but thought, he probably copied it from somewhere.
The next Wednesday. At the inter-house quiz, Leon's team won, and the chemistry teacher mentioned that Leon had moved because his father was transferred. Suraj shrugged. "Oh. Someone told me the cheating thing, I don't know who." Francis sat back. For nine days, one sentence on a bus had coloured everything Leon did.

qa.q: Why had Leon actually moved schools?
qa.a: Leon moved because his father was transferred.

qa.q: Why did Francis think Leon had probably copied the formula?
qa.a: Francis felt wary and suspicious because the first thing he heard about Leon was 'cheating', and that first label shaped how he read everything after.

qa.q: What could Francis do the next time he hears something about a person before meeting them?
qa.a: He could treat it as a rumour, ask where it came from, and judge the person by what he actually sees, like Leon's step-by-step help.

qa.q: What might those nine days have been like for Leon?
qa.a: Leon was new and probably felt the distance without knowing why, even while helping classmates.

grounding: Shows a teenager judging a new classmate by the first thing he heard about him, despite later evidence.

passage: Ojas, you always start your word list from the top, don't you? Your Omkar kaka did the same. So tonight, Ojas, start your list from the middle.

Last term I noticed something odd about the way my brain works. I'm Farhan, and I study by reading lists: the twenty causes of the revolt, the fifteen reactions in the chapter, that kind of thing.
In tests, I could always write the first four or five perfectly. The middle ones? Blank. It happened so often that my cousin Anirban started testing me from the bottom of the list first.
Then I noticed I do the same with people. Before our new maths teacher even arrived, a senior told me, "Strict, gives zero for late work." That was the first thing I heard. For months, every time she did something kind, like giving extra time to a boy with a broken arm, I thought, she's still strict. The first sentence had set like cement.
Now I shuffle my lists before I study. And I try to shuffle what I've heard about people too.

qa.a: Farhan's list had twenty causes of the revolt.

qa.q: Why did Farhan keep thinking the maths teacher was strict?
